tier_reason: The README Performance table lists absolute timings for internal components only: 83 ns p50 / 4.4 us p99.9 log append, 42 ns ring push+pop, 42 ns header decode, and <10 ms startup. benchmarks/latency_bench.cpp only times StrikeMQ's own ring buffer, log and codec. No Kafka number is measured or quoted anywhere (README, docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, PRODUCT.md, CHANGELOG.md or the Show HN post), so there is no comparative evidence against the baseline.
notes: The record's numbers and metadata are accurate: MIT, 14 stars, last commit 2026-02-12, not a fork, not archived, and CMake Release uses -O3 -march=native -flto. The Kafka contrast is only qualitative ('JVM, ZooKeeper/KRaft, gigabytes of RAM, slow startup'). The project is a dev/test stand-in, not a claimed faster broker, and it is also not notable (14 stars; the Show HN post got 3 points).

tier_reason: The README Benchmarks section runs binaryfuse against xor (and fuse) filters in one public harness, src/benchmark.zig. It states the compiler (Zig 0.12.0-dev.706+62a0fbdae), the flags (-O ReleaseFast) and the CPUs (AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, and a 2.3 GHz 8-core Intel Core i9 in a 2019 MacBook Pro). That meets A, although both sides are this library's own Zig implementations.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 2019 MacBook Pro (2.3 GHz 8-core Intel Core i9): binaryfuse8 builds a 1M-key filter in 37.5 ms vs 103.4 ms for xor8 (~2.8x) and a 100M-key filter in 7.4 s vs 28.0 s (~3.8x). Ryzen 9 3900X: 44.6 ms vs 76.0 ms at 1M (~1.7x) and 6.9 s vs 19.1 s at 100M (~2.8x). Ratios are derived from page data. contains() is about the same as xor8 (24.0 vs 25.0 ns at 1M and 145 vs 153 ns at 100M on the Mac). binaryfuse8 uses 9.04 vs 9.84 bits/key and 22 vs 52 MiB peak build memory at 1M.
corrections.hardware: 2019 MacBook Pro, 2.3 GHz 8-core Intel Core i9, 16 GB 2667 MHz DDR4; also Windows 10, 3.79 GHz AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, 32 GB 2133 MHz DDR4
corrections.caveats: Both sides of the comparison are this library's own Zig types (BinaryFuse vs Xor/Fuse) in the same harness. Nothing in this repo is measured against the C reference xor_singleheader, a Bloom filter or a cuckoo filter. The README's 'faster than Bloom, smaller than Cuckoo' line cites the Graf & Lemire papers, not local measurements. The published tables were made with Zig 0.12.0-dev.706. src/benchmark.zig has since been ported to newer Zig APIs, so the numbers do not come from the current code. contains() is no faster than xor; the win is build time and memory. The canonical source is now code.hexops.org (Forgejo, 0 stars). The GitHub repo hexops/fastfilter is archived (293 stars), not a redirect, and the README's build.zig.zon example still points to the GitHub archive URL.

notes: Downgraded for the overstated claim, not the tier. The record's '~19x-4x faster at 100M keys' is wrong: 28.0/7.4 is ~3.8x. 'i9-9900K-class' is also wrong, since the page gives only a 2.3 GHz 8-core i9 (a laptop part). The license (dual MIT/Apache-2.0 LICENSE files), the last commit (2026-04-11 UTC) and the GitHub mirror's 293 stars check out.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C. The README's generated 'Bench' section states the CPU (Apple M2 Max, macOS 26.5.1 arm64) and the compiler (rustc 1.98.0, 2026-08-18). The code is public (benches/comparison.rs run_bench_json, run by bench.sh via cargo bench --bench comparison, output in bench.json). The flags are in the workspace root Cargo.toml ([profile.bench] opt-level = 3). It runs against the named cuckoo-filter crates in the same harness.

corrections.baseline: cuckoo filter: sile's scalable_cuckoo_filter crate v0.5.1 (the upstream it was forked from, labelled 'cuckoo_filter' in the table) and the axiomhq cuckoofilter crate v0.5 with FarmHasher (~6M crates.io downloads)
corrections.claimed_speedup: README Bench section (Apple M2 Max, rustc 1.98.0; matches bench.json): contains 81.03 M/s vs 14.56 (scalable_cuckoo_filter) and 20.42 (cuckoofilter), ~5.6x/~4.0x. Add 21.83 vs 9.09/14.85 M/s, ~2.4x/~1.5x. Remove 53.55 vs 13.63/13.49 M/s, ~3.9x/~4.0x. The page's ratios are 0.18/0.25, 0.42/0.68 and 0.25/0.25. The earlier README Performance table, which states no environment, gives contains 77.32 vs 17.23/23.87, add 31.25 vs 10.38/23.84 and remove 48.36 vs 17.34/20.80 M/s. That table is the source of the '4.5x faster lookups, 3x faster additions/removals' marketing line.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.98.0 (88d9e12ae 2026-08-18); cargo bench --bench comparison with the workspace [profile.bench] opt-level = 3 (root Cargo.toml); mimalloc global allocator in the bench
corrections.hardware: Apple M2 Max (12 cores), 64 GB, macOS 26.5.1 arm64
corrections.workload: 100,000 generated byte-string keys. Each filter is sized for 200,000 at target FPP 0.01; cuckoofilter gets 1,000,000 capacity for a similar FPP. The bench times one Instant pass of add, then 1000 passes of contains over the same (all present) keys, then measures FPP with 100,000 other keys, then removes 10,000 keys (benches/comparison.rs run_bench_json -> bench.json).
corrections.caveats: The hasher differs per contender. autoscale defaults to gxhash (Cargo default feature, an AES-based hash; the README wrongly says RapidHash), scalable_cuckoo_filter uses its own default hasher, and cuckoofilter uses FarmHasher, so part of the gap is the hash function. contains measures only positive lookups. The table numbers come from single Instant-timed passes on one Apple M2 Max, not Criterion statistics. Measured FPP differs (0.17% vs 0.15% vs 0.27%), and cuckoofilter is given 10x capacity (1024 KB vs 353 KB). The upper README Performance table has no environment and disagrees with the generated Bench section and bench.json. The README says it was 'Forked from sile/cuckoo_filter', and that URL 301-redirects to sile/scalable_cuckoo_filter (MIT, 27 stars). It is a code copy, not a GitHub fork, relicensed as MulanPSL-2.0 (OSI-approved). No LICENSE file sits in the crate directory or the monorepo root; the license is declared only in Cargo.toml and the README. It lives in a monorepo with 3 stars and has 1,082 crates.io downloads.
